cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Drop the Armor
cards.instruction: Persuade someone to lower their guard, stop performing strength, or admit what affects them.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I'll decide how we handle this. You've locked the shop. You can stop doing the cheerful voice for me.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Someone has to keep morale up. You're my only employee.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You can question the details after my decision. I'm off the clock. What did that empty till do to you?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: I cried in the stockroom. Then I practised smiling.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You don't owe me a second performance. Can we lock the stockroom and let you be upset out here?

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 permits dropping voice and A3 rejects employee role off clock, but A5 can-we request does not sustain clear superior approval beyond the stock phrases.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 morale duty causes A3 off-clock question; B4 crying/smile rehearsal causes A5 permission to be upset publicly.

relationship.evidence: B2 feels responsible for the only employee and B4 admits hidden distress, giving a plausible reason for the performed strength.

heightening.evidence: B4 stockroom privacy causes A5 to move allowed vulnerability into the shared front space.

specificity.evidence: A1 locked shop and B2 employment establish actual rank; A can behave superior without actually owning the shop.

brevityWit.evidence: A5 no second performance is specific to B4 rehearsal but stock A3 command adds unevenness.
